claim: When placed off food, the foraging behavior of C. elegans can be described as a change between an initial local-search behavior characterized by a high rate of reorientations, followed by a global-search behavior characterized by sparse reorientations.
source: When placed off food, the foraging behavior of C. elegans can be described as a change between an initial local-search behavior characterized by a high rate of reorientations, followed by a global-search behavior characterized by sparse reorientations.
evidence: This is a statement about observed C. elegans behavior that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Only about half of C. elegans worms appear to exhibit the local-to-global search behavior transition when numerous worms are characterized.
source: This is commonly observed in individual worms, but when numerous worms are characterized, only about half appear to exhibit this behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from the experimental data analyzed in the study.

claim: A stochastic model that defines foraging reorientation rate as a decaying parameter can predict both abrupt and continuous changes to reorientation without relying on behavioral states.
source: We propose an alternative model that predicts both abrupt and continuous changes to reorientation that do not rely on behavioral states. This model is inspired by molecular dynamics modeling that defines the foraging reorientation rate as a decaying parameter.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis and model proposed by the authors, which is tested through computational modeling.

claim: Stochastically sampling from the time interval probability distribution defined by a decaying reorientation rate can produce both abrupt and gradual changes to reorientation rates, matching experimentally observed results.
source: By stochastically sampling from the time interval probability distribution defined by this rate, both abrupt and gradual changes to reorientation rates can occur, matching experimentally observed results.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The stochastic model does not depend on behavioral states or information accumulation.
source: Crucially, this model does not depend on behavioral states or information accumulation.
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed model as stated by the authors.

claim: Abrupt behavioral changes are not necessarily indicative of abrupt changes in behavioral states, especially when abrupt changes are not universally observed in the population.
source: Even though abrupt behavioral changes do occur, they are not necessarily indicative of abrupt changes in behavioral states, especially when abrupt changes are not universally observed in the population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results and experimental observations.

claim: Area Restricted Search (ARS) is a foraging strategy observed in nearly all animals.
source: A foraging strategy that is observed in nearly all animals is the Area Restricted Search (ARS) (Dorfman et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dorfman et al., 2022.

claim: In Area Restricted Search, animals randomly forage for food, but appetitive sensory cues cause the animal to restrict their search area by reorienting more frequently.
source: In ARS, animals randomly forage for food (Codling et al., 2008), but appetitive sensory cues (like an encounter with food) will cause the animal to restrict their search area by reorienting more frequently, thus increasing the likelihood of food encounters.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Codling et al., 2008 and represents established knowledge about ARS.

claim: When removed from food, animals decrease their reorientation rate to increase dispersal.
source: Conversely, when removed from food, animals will decrease their reorientation rate to increase dispersal (Reiss and Rankin, 2021; Klein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reiss and Rankin, 2021 and Klein et al., 2017.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila melanogaster larvae progressively increase their diffusion constant while foraging off of food by decreasing their rates of reorientation.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans and Drosophila melanogaster larvae appear to progressively increase their diffusion constant while foraging off of food by decreasing their rates of reorientation (Klein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2017.

claim: Individual C. elegans worms appear to make an abrupt change from a high to low rate of reorientation in separate studies.
source: However, in separate studies (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Calhoun et al., 2014), individual worms appear to make an abrupt change from a high to low rate of reorientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to López-Cruz et al., 2019 and Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: The abrupt change in reorientation behavior has been described as a switch from a local to global search strategy that relies on evidence accumulation to trigger the behavioral switch.
source: This behavior has been described as a switch from a local to global search strategy that relies on evidence accumulation to trigger the behavioral switch (Calhoun et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: Reorientations in C. elegans are random and follow Poisson statistics.
source: Reorientations are random and follow Poisson statistics (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2003; Stephens et al., 2011; Flavell et al., 2013; Gordus et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Iino and Yoshida, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The stochastic nature of reorientations is very similar to the temporal behavior of individual molecules in solution.
source: This is very similar to the temporal behavior of individual molecules in solution (Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2022 and represents an analogy drawn by the authors.

claim: Individual molecules defined by the same reaction kinetics can stochastically produce long or short time intervals between reaction events due to stochastic sampling from the same probability distribution.
source: Individual molecules defined by the same reaction kinetics can stochastically produce long or short time intervals between reaction events, not because one molecule is inherently faster than the other, but because they are stochastically sampling from the same probability distribution.
evidence: This is established knowledge from chemical kinetics used as an analogy.

claim: The exponentially decaying reorientation rate emerges from the average of trajectories that do not necessarily conform to this curve individually.
source: The exponentially decaying reorientation rate emerges from the average of trajectories that do not necessarily conform to this curve individually.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stochastic nature of the behavior.

claim: Abrupt changes in reorientation rates could be the result of stochastic sampling of an underlying decay phenomenon.
source: Since reorientations occur stochastically, the abrupt changes in reorientation rates could simply be the result of stochastic sampling of an underlying decay phenomenon (Srivastava et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, with a citation to Srivastava et al., 2009.

claim: A simple, stochastic model that does not rely on switches in behavioral state is sufficient to reproduce the reorientation kinetics observed in experimental data.
source: Here, we show that a simple, stochastic model that does not rely on switches in behavioral state is sufficient to reproduce the reorientation kinetics observed in experimental data.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the modeling results.

claim: In López-Cruz et al., 2019, the foraging behaviors of individual worms were tracked for 45 min after being removed from food.
source: In López-Cruz et al., 2019, the foraging behaviors of individual worms were tracked for 45 min after being removed from food.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: The reorientation rate from López-Cruz et al., 2019 followed an exponential decay.
source: As observed previously (Klein et al., 2017), the reorientation rate from this study followed an exponential decay (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and a citation to Klein et al., 2017.

claim: Roughly half the worms appeared to make a sudden single switch from local to global search as observed in Calhoun et al., 2014.
source: It was reported that roughly half the worms appeared to make a sudden single switch from local to global search as observed in Calhoun et al., 2014, however, the other half appeared to produce no discernible change in search strategy or exhibited multiple switches (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b-d and a citation to Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: The other half of worms appeared to produce no discernible change in search strategy or exhibited multiple switches.
source: It was reported that roughly half the worms appeared to make a sudden single switch from local to global search as observed in Calhoun et al., 2014, however, the other half appeared to produce no discernible change in search strategy or exhibited multiple switches (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1b-d.

claim: Whether or not a worm performed a single decision was defined in López-Cruz et al., 2019 by fitting individual reorientation data to two lines using the MATLAB function findchangepts.
source: Whether or not a worm performed a single decision was defined in López-Cruz et al., 2019 by fitting individual reorientation data to two lines using the MATLAB function findchangepts (Figure 1b; Killick et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in López-Cruz et al., 2019, with a citation to Killick et al., 2012.

claim: The findchangepts function divides each trace into two regions that are defined by minimizing the sum of the residual squared error of two local linear regressions.
source: This function divides each trace into two regions that are defined by minimizing the sum of the residual squared error of two local linear regressions.
evidence: This describes how the findchangepts function works.

claim: The location of the transition point is varied until the total residual error attains a minimum.
source: The location of the transition point is varied until the total residual error attains a minimum (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the optimization process of the findchangepts function.

claim: A large change in slope indicates a sudden change in reorientation rate, and the intersection between the two lines determines the decision time.
source: A large change in slope indicates a sudden change in reorientation rate, and the intersection between the two lines determines the decision time (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the findchangepts results as used in López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: A worm was identified as making a sudden local-to-global foraging switch based on visually assessing the magnitude of the slope difference.
source: A worm was identified as making a sudden local-to-global foraging switch based on visually assessing the magnitude of the slope difference, therefore, the conclusion that 50% of the worms produced a single transition is fairly subjective.
evidence: This describes the subjective nature of the classification method used in López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: The conclusion that 50% of the worms produced a single transition is fairly subjective.
source: A worm was identified as making a sudden local-to-global foraging switch based on visually assessing the magnitude of the slope difference, therefore, the conclusion that 50% of the worms produced a single transition is fairly subjective.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors of the methodology used in prior work.

claim: The distributions of slope differences (s1-s2) and transition times for the experimental data were continuous, with no clear boundary between deciders and non-deciders.
source: The resulting distributions for the experimental data were continuous, with no clear boundary between deciders and non-deciders (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The Gillespie algorithm is a common strategy used to model the kinetics of individual molecules.
source: We tested this hypothesis by modeling individual worms by stochastic sampling of a decaying reorientation rate with the Gillespie algorithm (Figure 2a), a common strategy used to model the kinetics of individual molecules (Gillespie, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gillespie, 1977.

claim: With the Gillespie algorithm, the time between chemical events is modeled by randomly sampling from the time-interval distributions defined by the reaction rates.
source: With this strategy, the time between chemical events is modeled by randomly sampling from the time-interval distributions defined by the reaction rates.
evidence: This describes how the Gillespie algorithm works.

claim: The Gillespie algorithm can be used to generate time trajectories for any discrete events when the kinetics are known.
source: Although the algorithm was originally developed to model discrete molecular events based on known kinetic parameters, it can be used to generate time trajectories for any discrete events when the kinetics are known.
evidence: This is a general statement about the applicability of the Gillespie algorithm.

claim: Stochastic fluctuations of predator and prey populations in the Lotka-Volterra model can be modeled using the Gillespie algorithm.
source: Stochastic fluctuations of predator and prey populations can be modeled using the Gillespie algorithm (Palombi et al., 2020; Reichenbach et al., 2006; Constable and McKane, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Palombi et al., 2020, Reichenbach et al., 2006, and Constable and McKane, 2015.

claim: The parameters α, β, and γ were assigned based on fitting a decay curve to the observed average reorientation rate.
source: In our approach, we fit the exponential curve in Equation 2 to the average reorientation rate from the experimental data from López-Cruz (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Figure 2b), and then used these parameters (α, β, γ) to model 1631 individual worms (the same number of animals in the experimental data).
evidence: This describes the methodology used to parameterize the model.

claim: 1631 individual worms were modeled, the same number of animals in the experimental data.
source: In our approach, we fit the exponential curve in Equation 2 to the average reorientation rate from the experimental data from López-Cruz (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Figure 2b), and then used these parameters (α, β, γ) to model 1631 individual worms (the same number of animals in the experimental data).
evidence: This describes the sample size used in the modeling.

claim: There is considerable variance in observed initial reorientation rates even though the initial average rates are ~1.5 events/minute.
source: Even though the initial average rates of reorientation are ~1.5 events/minute, there is considerable variance in observed initial rates (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Starting values of M were assigned based on randomly drawing a rate from the observed experimental rates at t=0, and adjusting M so that the starting rate for that in silico worm matched the initial rate of the randomly drawn experimental worm.
source: To address this variance, starting values of M were assigned based on randomly drawing a rate from the observed experimental rates at t=0, and adjusting M so that the starting rate for that in silico worm j matched the initial rate of the randomly drawn experimental worm
evidence: This describes the methodology for initializing the model.

claim: In silico reorientation curves generated produced single-transition and multi/absent transition curves, as observed experimentally.
source: In silico reorientation curves generated produced single-transition and multi/absent transition curves, as observed experimentally (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The in silico data produced a distribution of linear regression parameters comparable to the experimental worms.
source: When plotted along with the experimental data, the in silico data produced a distribution of linear regression parameters comparable to the experimental worms (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The simulation was able to produce individual trajectories that demonstrated switching behavior, despite the lack of a switching mechanism in the model.
source: The simulation was able to produce individual trajectories that demonstrated switching behavior, despite the lack of a switching mechanism in the model (Equations 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a key finding of the modeling study.

claim: The model demonstrated a continuum of switching to non-switching behavior that was observed in experimental results.
source: Furthermore, our model demonstrated a continuum of switching to non-switching behavior that was observed in experimental results (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The experimental transition distribution was shifted slightly earlier compared to the model.
source: The experimental transition distribution was shifted slightly earlier, however, it is important to note that the experimental data were drawn from experiments where 10–15 animals were tracked together.
evidence: This is an observation about the difference between experimental and model data.

claim: In the experimental data, 10-15 animals were tracked together.
source: The experimental transition distribution was shifted slightly earlier, however, it is important to note that the experimental data were drawn from experiments where 10–15 animals were tracked together.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Collisions occurred in the experiments but were excluded from analysis.
source: Collisions occurred, but were excluded from analysis, and so would not contribute to this observation.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Animals reorient in response to pheromones when they cross the tracks left by other animals, which is more likely early in the recording when the animals are in close proximity.
source: However, in addition to collisions, animals also reorient in response to pheromones when they cross the tracks left by other animals, which is more likely early in the recording when the animals are in close proximity (Hong et al., 2017; Dal Bello et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hong et al., 2017 and Dal Bello et al., 2021.

claim: Pheromone track crossing may contribute to a higher initial rate early in the experimental observations, which would delay the observed decay in reorientations.
source: This, in turn, may contribute to a higher initial rate early in the experimental observations, which would delay the observed decay in reorientations.
evidence: This is an inference about how pheromone effects could influence the experimental results.

claim: Modeling worm foraging behavior with a simple exponential decay of reorientations was sufficient to capture most experimentally observed dynamics, both switch and non-switch-like.
source: This exception aside, modeling worm foraging behavior with a simple exponential decay of reorientations was sufficient to capture most experimentally observed dynamics, both switch and non-switch-like.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Sudden switches between fast and slow reorientation rates were observed in both the experimental and modeled data.
source: Sudden switches between fast and slow reorientation rates were observed in both the experimental and modeled data (Figure 2e), despite the model not relying on a switch strategy, and the decay in M being continuous.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The model does not rely on a switch strategy, and the decay in M is continuous.
source: Sudden switches between fast and slow reorientation rates were observed in both the experimental and modeled data (Figure 2e), despite the model not relying on a switch strategy, and the decay in M being continuous.
evidence: This describes key features of the model.

claim: The stochastic model produced reorientation data with similar dynamics to experimental data, despite not relying on a decision paradigm.
source: The stochastic model produced reorientation data with similar dynamics, despite not relying on a decision paradigm.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: The model was not explicitly designed to match the sudden changes in reorientation rates observed in the experimental data.
source: It is important to emphasize that the model was not explicitly designed to match the sudden changes in reorientation rates observed in the experimental data.
evidence: This clarifies the modeling approach.

claim: Kinetic parameters were simply chosen to match the average population behavior.
source: Kinetic parameters were simply chosen to match the average population behavior.
evidence: This describes the modeling methodology.

claim: Sudden changes in reorientation rate were not due to sudden changes in the underlying model; stochastic behavior naturally produces sudden bunching of random events.
source: Sudden changes in reorientation rate were not due to sudden changes in the underlying model; stochastic behavior naturally produces sudden bunching of random events.
evidence: This is a key insight from the modeling results.

claim: Even if the reorientation rate is set to a constant value, stochastic sampling will still produce sudden changes in rate.
source: Even if the reorientation rate is set to a constant value, stochastic sampling will still produce sudden changes in rate, even though the rate has no time-dependence (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: A large initial value for M0 (M0=1000) was initially chosen to ensure a smooth change in reorientation rate.
source: A large initial value for M0 (M0=1000) was initially chosen to ensure a smooth change in reorientation rate, so that sudden changes in reorientation number were not necessarily due to sudden changes in M.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the modeling choice.

claim: All values of M0 (1000, 100, 10, or 1) were sufficient to reproduce the average reorientation decay observed in experimental data.
source: On average, all values of M0 were sufficient to reproduce the average reorientation decay observed in experimental data (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The distributions of transition times and slope differences were comparable for M0=1000, 100, or 10.
source: The distributions of transition times and slope differences were also comparable for M0=1000, 100, or 10, indicating that the model is not particularly sensitive to initial values of M0.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results.

claim: The model is not particularly sensitive to initial values of M0 (for M0=1000, 100, or 10).
source: The distributions of transition times and slope differences were also comparable for M0=1000, 100, or 10, indicating that the model is not particularly sensitive to initial values of M0.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The distribution of slope differences was distinctly bimodal for M0=1.
source: However, despite producing a similar average decay in reorientation rates, the distribution of slope differences was distinctly bimodal for M0=1 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When M0=1, the model is by definition a two-state system.
source: This was not surprising, since when M0=1, the model is by definition a two-state system.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model structure.

claim: In the M0=1 model, either the worm has a reorientation rate of α+β (M=1), or a reorientation rate of β (M=0).
source: Either the worm has a reorientation rate of α+β (M=1), or a reorientation rate of β (M=0).
evidence: This describes the two-state nature of the M0=1 model.

claim: The probability of switching from M=1 to M=0 increases with a timescale of γ (γ=0.11 min–1).
source: The probability of switching from M=1 to M=0 increases with a timescale of γ (γ=0.11 min–1).
evidence: This describes the dynamics of the M0=1 model.

claim: The bimodal slope and transition time distributions for M0=1 were distinctly different from those observed for the experimental or M0=1000, 100, 10 models.
source: The bimodal slope and transition time distributions for M0=1 were distinctly different from those observed for the experimental or M0=1000, 100, 10 models.
evidence: This is an observation from the modeling results.

claim: The non-binary models (M0≠1) all produced comparable Jensen-Shannon divergence distances to the experimental data.
source: The non-binary models (M0≠ 1) all produced comparable distances, but the binary models (M0=1) were significantly more distant than the rest, indicating this model was more dissimilar than the others when compared to the experimental data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Jensen-Shannon divergence analysis.

claim: The binary models (M0=1) were significantly more distant than the non-binary models when compared to the experimental data.
source: The non-binary models (M0≠ 1) all produced comparable distances, but the binary models (M0=1) were significantly more distant than the rest, indicating this model was more dissimilar than the others when compared to the experimental data.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Jensen-Shannon divergence analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: A continuous decline in reorientation rate is more consistent with experimental observations than a discrete change in reorientation rate.
source: A continuous decline in reorientation rate is more consistent with experimental observations than a discrete change in reorientation rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The lack of a decision simplifies the dispersal strategy for C. elegans.
source: The lack of a decision simplifies the dispersal strategy for C. elegans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Rather than relying on the accumulation of evidence to make a discrete decision, the worm relies on a decaying signal in the absence of food that drives the reorientation rate.
source: Rather than relying on the accumulation of evidence to make a discrete decision, the worm relies on a decaying signal in the absence of food that drives the reorientation rate.
evidence: This is the proposed alternative mechanism based on the modeling results.

claim: The decaying signal strategy increases the diffusion constant of the worm, and ensures a more efficient search strategy to find food.
source: This strategy increases the diffusion constant of the worm, and ensures a more efficient search strategy to find food (Klein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2017.

claim: The stochastic nature of the search is consistent with prior characterizations of worm behavior and neuronal dynamics.
source: The stochastic nature of this search is consistent with prior characterizations of worm behavior and neuronal dynamics (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2003; Stephens et al., 2011; Flavell et al., 2013; Gordus et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Iino and Yoshida, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Any individual worm would exhibit all the variability of the population if allowed to perform the foraging task multiple times.
source: The stochastic nature of this search is consistent with prior characterizations of worm behavior and neuronal dynamics (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2003; Stephens et al., 2011; Flavell et al., 2013; Gordus et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Iino and Yoshida, 2009), and implies that any individual worm would exhibit all the variability of the population if allowed to perform this task multiple times.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stochastic nature of the behavior.

claim: Simple stochastic models should be sufficient to explain observable stochastic behaviors (null model).
source: We consider this to be a null model: simple stochastic models should be sufficient to explain observable stochastic behaviors.
evidence: This is a philosophical statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The decay in M can be considered the memory timescale of the last food encounter.
source: The decay in M can be considered the memory timescale of the last food encounter.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what M represents biologically.

claim: With an observed γ of 0.07 min–1, the memory timescale τ1/2 is ~10 min.
source: With an observed γ of 0.07 min–1, this would mean a memory τ1/2 of ~10 min.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the fitted parameter γ.

claim: In principle, M should rise in the presence of food to increase the reorientation rate, on a timescale that is not addressed in this study.
source: In principle, M should rise in the presence of food to increase the reorientation rate, on a timescale that is not addressed here.
evidence: This is speculation about how M would behave in the presence of food.

claim: In López-Cruz et al., 2019, the starting reorientation rate correlated with food density prior to food removal.
source: In López-Cruz et al., 2019, the starting reorientation rate correlated with food density prior to food removal, which would be consistent with the amplitude of M correlating with food density/quality.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: The amplitude of M correlating with food density/quality would be consistent with the observation that starting reorientation rate correlated with food density prior to food removal.
source: In López-Cruz et al., 2019, the starting reorientation rate correlated with food density prior to food removal, which would be consistent with the amplitude of M correlating with food density/quality.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the model to experimental observations.

claim: The reliance of the reorientation rate while foraging for food on a decaying factor (M) implies that the rate is influenced by a signaling factor which decays in time.
source: The reliance of the reorientation rate while foraging for food on a decaying factor (M) implies that the rate is influenced by a signaling factor which decays in time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model in biological terms.

claim: It is well established that the reorientation rate is influenced by numerous signaling factors and is the basis of the biased random walk that drives taxis in shallow gradients.
source: It is well established that the reorientation rate is influenced by numerous signaling factors and is the basis of the biased random walk that drives taxis in shallow gradients (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Zhao et al., 2003; Stephens et al., 2011; Flavell et al., 2013; Gordus et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Iino and Yoshida, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: A decay in reorientation rate, rather than a sudden change, is consistent with observations made by López-Cruz et al., 2019.
source: A decay in reorientation rate, rather than a sudden change, is consistent with observations made by López-Cruz et al., 2019.
evidence: This connects the model to experimental observations.

claim: The neurons AIA and ADE redundantly suppress reorientations.
source: They found that the neurons AIA and ADE redundantly suppress reorientations, and that silencing either one was sufficient to restore the large number of reorientations during early foraging.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: Silencing either AIA or ADE was sufficient to restore the large number of reorientations during early foraging.
source: They found that the neurons AIA and ADE redundantly suppress reorientations, and that silencing either one was sufficient to restore the large number of reorientations during early foraging.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: The timescale of the variable M may represent the timescales of AIA and ADE activities.
source: This implies that the timescale of the variable M may represent the timescales of AIA and ADE activities.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the model to neuronal mechanisms.

claim: AIA and ADE synapse onto several neurons that drive reorientations.
source: AIA and ADE synapse onto several neurons that drive reorientations (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Gray et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to López-Cruz et al., 2019 and Gray et al., 2005.

claim: The output of AIA and ADE was inhibited over long timescales (tens of minutes) by presynaptic glutamate binding to MGL-1, a slow G-protein coupled receptor expressed in AIA and ADE.
source: AIA and ADE synapse onto several neurons that drive reorientations (López-Cruz et al., 2019; Gray et al., 2005), and their output was inhibited over long timescales (tens of minutes) by presynaptic glutamate binding to MGL-1, a slow G-protein coupled receptor expressed in AIA and ADE.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: Sensory neurons suppress the synaptic output of AIA and ADE, which leads to a large number of reorientations early in foraging.
source: Their results support a model where sensory neurons suppress the synaptic output of AIA and ADE, which in turn leads to a large number of reorientations early in foraging.
evidence: This is a model supported by results from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: As time passes, glutamatergic input from the sensory neurons decreases, which leads to disinhibition of AIA and ADE and a subsequent suppression of reorientations.
source: As time passes, glutamatergic input from the sensory neurons decreases, which leads to disinhibition of AIA and ADE and a subsequent suppression of reorientations.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model supported by López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claim: The sensory inputs into AIA and ADE are sequestered into two separate circuits, with AIA receiving chemosensory input and ADE receiving mechanosensory input.
source: The sensory inputs into AIA and ADE are sequestered into two separate circuits, with AIA receiving chemosensory input and ADE receiving mechanosensory input.
evidence: This describes the neural circuit organization.

claim: Since the suppression of either AIA or ADE is sufficient to increase reorientations, the decay in reorientations is likely due to the suppression of both of these neurons decaying in time.
source: Since the suppression of either AIA or ADE is sufficient to increase reorientations, the decay in reorientations is likely due to the suppression of both of these neurons decaying in time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the redundant function of AIA and ADE.

claim: The timescale of reorientation decay could be tied to the timescale of sensory neuron activity, which in turn is influencing the timescale of AIA/ADE reorientation suppression.
source: This correlates with an observed decrease in sensory neuron activity as well, so the timescale of reorientation decay could be tied to the timescale of sensory neuron activity, which in turn is influencing the timescale of AIA/ADE reorientation suppression.
evidence: This is an inference connecting multiple levels of the neural mechanism.

claim: The factor 'M' is likely the sum of several different sensory inputs decaying in time.
source: This implies that our factor 'M' is likely the sum of several different sensory inputs decaying in time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what M represents biologically.

claim: The glutamatergic input provided by the sensory neurons was not essential for AIA/ADE signaling.
source: The molecular basis of which sensory neuron signaling factors contribute to decreased AIA and ADE activity is made more complicated by the observation that the glutamatergic input provided by the sensory neurons was not essential, and that additional factors besides glutamate contribute to the signaling to AIA and ADE.

claim: Additional factors besides glutamate contribute to the signaling to AIA and ADE.
